title: Data Consistency Models
description: Learn about consistency models in distributed systems and their implications for microservices.

data.text: In a distributed system, maintaining data consistency across services is challenging. Amazon, Google, and Netflix all had to make trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance as defined by the CAP theorem.

The CAP theorem states that a distributed system can provide at most two of the three guarantees: Consistency (all nodes see the same data), Availability (every request receives a response), and Partition Tolerance (system works despite network failures). In practice, network partitions happen, so you must choose between consistency and availability.

data.title: From Strong to Eventual
items: Strong consistency: All nodes see the same data at the same time
Causal consistency: Related operations appear in order
Eventual consistency: Nodes may temporarily diverge but eventually converge
Read-your-writes: A client always sees its own writes

data.title: Real-World Implication
data.text: Amazon's shopping cart uses eventual consistency. If you add an item in one tab, it may not appear immediately in another tab. Most users accept this minor inconsistency for better availability.

data.title: Example: Consistency Trade-offs
data.code: Compare strong consistency (banking) vs eventual consistency (social media).

# Banking: Strong consistency required
# - Account balance must be accurate everywhere
# - Two-phase commit or distributed transactions
# - Sacrifice availability during network partitions

# Social media: Eventual consistency acceptable
# - Like counts can be slightly delayed
# - Use eventual consistency for high availability
# - Background jobs reconcile differences

data.caption: CAP theorem trade-offs
data.definition:
graph TD
    C[CAP Theorem] --> CP[CP: Consistency + Partition Tolerance]
    C --> AP[AP: Availability + Partition Tolerance]
    C --> CA[CA: Consistency + Availability]
    CP -->|Banking systems| B[Choose when data accuracy is critical]
    AP -->|Social media, e-commerce| S[Choose when availability is critical]
    CA -->|Not practical in distributed systems| N[Network partitions will occur]

items.question: Which consistency model should I use?
items.answer: Start with the strongest consistency your domain requires. Banking needs strong consistency; social media can tolerate eventual consistency.

items.question: What is the PACELC theorem?
items.answer: PACELC extends CAP by stating that even without partitions (EL), you must choose between latency and consistency.

items.question: Can I change consistency models later?
items.answer: Yes, but it is difficult. Design for eventual consistency from the start if you anticipate scaling; you can always add stronger consistency where needed.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: CAP theorem: Choose consistency or availability during partitions
Eventual consistency is acceptable for many domains
Use stronger consistency for critical data like payments
data.takeaway: Choose the weakest consistency model your domain can tolerate; stronger consistency adds latency and complexity.
